## Two layers, and they answer DIFFERENT questions
Cloudflare Access Service Auth (in front, `/webhook/owner-*`) answers **which machine**. The HMAC here answers **which request**. Both are required: if the service token ever leaks, the signature is the only thing left standing.

Raw body ON — the signature is over the exact bytes the dashboard sent.

## The allow-list is the security model
Exactly ONE verb: `release_handoff`. `prompt-injection.md` — there is no other write action, so there is nothing for a compromise to escalate into. This is also why CRT #11 is auditable: the surface is one verb.

Mirrors `OWNER_ACTIONS` in `lib/ownerAction.ts`. Two places, on purpose.

## A signature does not say WHICH conversation
Three conditions, all required: the record exists · `stage === 'handoff'` · touched within 30 days. Otherwise 404 (missing) / 409 (not locked).

Without this, one valid signature unlocks ARBITRARY conversations — the same hole the endpoint exists to close, just moved inside the fence.

## Replay: the honest bound
The dedupe row is written at the END. A replay arriving while the first is STILL IN FLIGHT finds nothing and proceeds.

What makes that safe is that the write is IDEMPOTENT — `stage='new'` twice equals once. There is no calendar-id backstop here like the booking path has. Do NOT read this as "deduplicated".

## Write-then-verify
Airtable and the engine share no transaction. A 200 is not a confirmed write — `booking-integrity.md` requires the re-read on every mutation path.

`stage` AND `last_intent` TOGETHER: two escalation ladders read `last_intent`, so clearing only `stage` leaves the conversation half-armed and it re-locks on the next uncertain turn.

## Failure is VISIBLE
A release that did not happen must never look like one that did. Separate alert class, separate branch, 502 to the caller.

⚠ This leaf is TERMINAL — no alert about a failed alert (infinite loop).
